blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we dive to the bottom of the sea, then visit a rainforest leaf.
Our first hero lives beside hot water, two thousand five hundred metres under the sea.
Our second hero is no bigger than your fingernail — but it knows a disappearing trick that surprises even scientists.
Let's go!
Deep under the Pacific Ocean, where no sunlight comes, hot water erupts from cracks in the seafloor.
These are hydrothermal vents — underwater hot springs, made where seawater meets hot rock below.
Around the vents crowd giant tube worms and mussels, fed by tiny bacteria that live on the hot chemicals, not sunlight.
It takes courage to explore a world no human can visit.
Their ship waited far above, its engine humming, while their robot, SuBastian, did the diving.
It sank two thousand five hundred metres to a volcano on the East Pacific Rise.
It lifted heavy pieces of volcanic rock — and underneath, to the delight of the team, it found warm, hidden caves.
Inside those caves, at twenty-five degrees, lived animals no one had expected: young tube worms and small snails, in the dark below the seafloor.
The team also found a clue to an old mystery: baby tube worms are almost never seen above the vents.
Now scientists think it is no coincidence — the babies travel under the seafloor, through warm water in the cracks, to start new homes.
Now meet a frog that can almost disappear.
The glassfrog lives in the rainforests of Central and South America.
It is small and green, and its flesh is so clear you can see its heart and stomach right through it — like looking through glass.
By day, it sleeps on the underside of a leaf, where hungry birds could easily spot it.
So how does it stay safe?
Scientists found the answer with a special camera that can see blood moving inside the body.
When the glassfrog sleeps, it packs almost ninety percent of its red blood cells into its liver, hidden behind tiny mirror-like crystals.
With the red cells out of the way, light passes through the frog's body, and it becomes two or three times more see-through — it simply fades into the leaf.
Their primary job, carrying oxygen, can wait until the frog wakes up.
When it wakes, the cells rush back into the blood in seconds, and it can jump away.
Most animals could never do this safely — but the glassfrog does it every day, and its trick may teach doctors new ideas about blood.
Here's today's idiom: "read between the lines." Words on a page say one thing — but the real message may hide between the lines.
If you read between the lines, you notice clues and understand what is not said.
The deep-sea scientists did just that: they read between the lines of the ocean's clues and found a hidden world.
Here's an example: "When Mia said she was 'fine' with a tiny smile, I read between the lines — she was sad." What hidden messages have you found?
Let's think about our stories.
We found a hidden world under deep-sea vents, and a frog that turns almost invisible.
Now, two questions for you.
First: if you could explore the deep sea in a robot, what would you look for first?
Second: if you could turn invisible for one day, where would you hide?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Like the deep-sea scientists, read between the lines — and keep exploring.
See you tomorrow morning!
